title: 'It's hard to know who is covering whose butt' in mass shooting probe: psychologist
article: A week after the federal and provincial justice ministers said they would hold a review behind closed doors of the April 18-19 rampage out of respect for the families who'd asked for something entirely different, it devolved into finger-pointing.
Faced with widespread outrage, provincial Justice Minister Mark Furey and Premier Stephen McNeil appeared to blame it on the feds on Tuesday.

Liberal MPs and senators from Atlantic Canada broke ranks and at 5 p.m. on Tuesday federal Public Safety Minister Bill Blair announced via a Tweet in French that a public inquiry would indeed be held.
"It's hard to know who is covering whose butt here, isn't it," said Stephen Perrott, a clinical psychologist at Mount Saint Vincent University and a 10-year veteran of Halifax Regional Police.

Neither Perrott nor Saint Mary's University criminologist Stephen Schneider think we should yield to grand conspiracies as we begin the long wait for an announced but as yet unscheduled public inquiry.
For context, the Desmond Inquiry into the January 2017 killing by Afghan War veteran Lionel Demond of his wife, Shanna, mother Brenda and daughter Aaliyah, only began last winter.
"They are always very complicated and costly," Schneider said about government apprehension over a public inquiry.
"I think it may be a little too early to jump to conclusions that government is trying to hide something or protect the RCMP."

While politicians were avoiding the public inquiry being demanded by victims' families, legal scholars and citizens, the RCMP was fighting media (including The Chronicle Herald) in court to keep the warrants sealed that it used to get access to the shooter's home and business after the incident.

The details they didn't think the rest of us should know, but Provincial Court Judge Laurel Halfpenney MacQuarrie did, included allegations that the shooter had smuggled drugs and guns from Maine for years and was a sexual predator.
An acquaintance of the shooter told them he was "controlling and paranoid" and would talk of "getting rid of bodies, burning and chemicals."

While those details were provided to the RCMP in interviews after the shooting occurred, in 2011 a notice was sent out to policing agencies province-wide by the Truro Police Service that the perpetrator had illegal guns and wanted "to kill a cop."
The perpetrator's home in Portapique, however, was in the RCMP's jurisdiction.
Then there was a MacLean's article detailing how the shooter withdrew $475,000 from a CIBC Intria Account days before his rampage. Those accounts are not available to private citizens.

"Sources in both banking and the RCMP say the transaction is consistent with how the RCMP funnels money to its confidential informants and agents, and is not an option available to private banking customers," read that article.
The RCMP has publicly denied that the shooter was on their payroll.
Schneider called the associations made by the article "highly speculative."
"It's not atypical for RCMP to use a criminal as an informant," added Schneider. "But (the article is a) long ways away from establishing he was an RCMP informant."
A request for comment Tuesday by The Chronicle Herald to the RCMP on what it knew about the shooter prior to April 18 went unanswered.
"The most famous line from police is 'we can't release information on a matter under investigation,'" said Perrott.
"The fact police will not give any more information than they absolutely have to is not surprising. The question is why did the government follow suit?"
For an answer to that question, it appears we will have to wait.
Though he expects the RCMP to get exposed to a lot of criticism over mistakes made, he cautions that police were dealing with an evolving situation with limited information and resources.
"This was the largest mass murder in Canadian history. How do you plan for that? You can't," said Perrott.
